steps.title: Picture it
steps.narration: One bag has three packs. Each pack has three boxes. Each box has three sweets. Three keeps multiplying itself as you count through the layers.

steps.title: Combine powers with the same base
steps.narration: A power is just a short way of writing repeated multiplication. Two cubed means three twos multiplied together. So if you multiply two cubed by two to the four, how many twos do you have? Three plus four, seven twos. That is why you add the powers. Dividing cancels some twos, so you subtract. This only works when the bases are the same.

steps.title: Apply an outer power
steps.narration: What happens when you raise a power to another power? Two cubed, squared, means two cubed written twice. That is three twos, then three more. Six twos in total. So you multiply the powers. And when the bracket holds a product or a fraction, the outer power goes to every part inside.

steps.title: Use zero and negative powers
steps.narration: Where does power zero come from? Divide five cubed by five cubed. You get one, because anything divided by itself is one. But the power rule says three minus three, which is zero. So five to the zero must be one. A negative power means flip it. Two to the minus three is one over eight.

steps.title: Read a fractional exponent as a root
steps.narration: A fraction in the power is a root and a power together. The bottom number is the root. The top number is the power. For twenty seven to the two thirds, the bottom is three, so take the cube root first. That gives three. Then the top is two, so square it. Three squared is nine. Root first keeps the numbers small.

steps.title: Match the bases before solving
steps.narration: If two powers of the same base are equal, their powers must be equal too. So the trick is to make the bases match. Four to the x equals eight looks hard. But four is two squared, and eight is two cubed. Now both sides are powers of two, so two x equals three. That gives one and a half.

steps.title: Normalise standard form
steps.narration: Standard form is a short way to write very big or very small numbers. Look at the front number. It must be at least one but less than ten. So twelve times ten to the five is not finished, because twelve is too big. Make it one point two, and give the ten one more power. Now it is one point two times ten to the six.

steps.title: Spot the fraction in the power
steps.narration: Let's try one. Three things are hiding in this power. A minus sign, a bottom number four, and a top number three. Take them one at a time, starting with the bottom. The bottom number means the fourth root. What number times itself four times gives sixteen? Two. So the fourth root of sixteen is two.

steps.title: Use the numerator as a power
steps.narration: Now the top number, three. It means we cube our answer. Two cubed is eight. So sixteen to the three quarters is eight. We have used the bottom and the top. Only the minus sign is left.

steps.title: Take the reciprocal
steps.narration: A minus sign in the power means flip it over. So eight becomes one over eight. That is the answer. Notice the order we used. Root, then power, then flip. It keeps the numbers small, so you never have to work with big ones.

steps.title: Rewrite using base three
steps.narration: Now a real JAMB question. The bases are different, twenty seven, nine and three. We can't compare them like that. But all three come from three. Twenty seven is three cubed. Nine is three squared. So let's write everything with base three.

steps.title: Multiply the inner and outer powers
steps.narration: Twenty seven to the x plus two becomes three cubed, to the x plus two. A power of a power, so multiply. That is three to the three times x plus two. Do the same for nine. It becomes three to the two times x plus one. Keep the brackets for now.

steps.title: Subtract the whole denominator exponent
steps.narration: Dividing powers with the same base means subtract the powers. Here is the trap. You must subtract the whole bottom power, not just part of it. Three x plus six, minus two x, minus two. That leaves x plus four. The brackets protect you from a sign mistake.

steps.title: Compare the exponents
steps.narration: Now both sides are three to some power. So the powers must be equal. X plus four equals two x. Take x from both sides, and x is four. Check it. Four plus four is eight, and two times four is eight. Both match, so we are right.

steps.title: Check both exponents
steps.narration: JAMB likes to offer an answer that looks close. If you try three, the left power becomes seven but the right becomes six. Not equal, so three is wrong. Always put your answer back in and check both powers. It takes ten seconds and saves the mark.

steps.title: Check the sign in standard form
steps.narration: In standard form, a number smaller than one needs a negative power of ten. Zero point eight six is less than one. So it is eight point six times ten to the minus one, not ten to the one. Ask yourself, is my number big or small? Then check the sign.

steps.title: Remember this
steps.narration: So here is the one habit for indices. Make the bases the same, then follow what happens to the powers. Multiplying adds them. Dividing subtracts them. A bracket multiplies them. Keep track of the power, and indices become simple.

quickCheck.stem: Write \frac{0.0001432}{1940000} as k × 10^{n}, where 1 ≤ k < 10 and n is an integer. Give k to three decimal places.

options.why: The coefficient rounds to 7.381 after normalising the quotient, and the power of ten is −11.
Dividing the powers gives 10^{-10} before normalising, so a positive exponent has the wrong scale.
A power of 2 would make the quotient much larger than 1, although the numerator is smaller than the denominator.
The exponent is right, but 1.432 ÷ 1.94 ≈ 0.738144, which normalises to a coefficient of 7.381.

steps.title: Picture it
steps.narration: You start with one sweet and double your pile each round. When you reach eight sweets, a logarithm tells you how many doublings it took.

steps.title: Read a logarithm as an exponent
working: log A = log_{10} A in common logarithm notation; ln A = log_{e} A
steps.narration: A logarithm is a question. Log base two of eight asks, what power of two gives eight? Two times two times two is eight. Three twos, so the answer is three. Every log is really a power in disguise. Log of one is always zero, and log of the base itself is always one. A log with no base written means base ten.

steps.title: Combine logs with the same base
steps.narration: Logs turn multiplying into adding. Why? Because a log is a power, and multiplying powers adds them. So log of A plus log of B is log of A times B. Taking away logs means dividing inside. Log two of eight minus log two of two is log two of four. That is two.

steps.title: Move a multiplier into the power
steps.narration: A number in front of a log can climb up into the power. Two times log of three becomes log of three squared. It works the other way too. Half of log sixteen becomes log of root sixteen. This is useful for combining logs. Move every front number into the power first, then combine.

steps.title: Change to a convenient base
steps.narration: Sometimes the base is awkward. Change it to one you like. Log base four of sixty four looks hard. But four and sixty four are both powers of two. So write it as log two of sixty four over log two of four. That is six over two, which is three. Choose a base that makes both numbers easy.

steps.title: Solve within the original domain
steps.display: log_{b} u = log_{b} v ⇒ u = v (u > 0, v > 0)
steps.narration: When you solve a log equation, you must remember one rule. You can only take the log of a positive number. So write down what x is allowed to be before you start. Then undo the log by writing it as a power. Log base three of x minus one equals two means x minus one is nine.

steps.title: Start with the allowed values
steps.narration: Let's try one. Before any working, ask which values of x are allowed. Log of x needs x bigger than zero. Log of x minus two needs x bigger than two. So x must be bigger than two. Keep that rule, because we will need it at the end.

steps.title: Combine and undo the logarithm
steps.narration: Two logs added with the same base. Adding logs means multiplying inside. So we get log two of x times x minus two, equals three. Now undo the log. What does it mean? Two to the power three gives x times x minus two. So x times x minus two equals eight.

steps.title: Factor and test the candidates
steps.narration: Expand and you get a quadratic. Move the eight across and factorise. You get x minus four, times x plus two. So x could be four or minus two. Now remember our rule. X must be bigger than two. Minus two breaks the rule, so throw it away. The answer is four. Check it, and it works.

steps.title: Start with the first log
steps.narration: Now a real JAMB question. It looks scary, with three logs and a fraction for a base. But we just take each log alone. Start with log three of twenty seven. What power of three gives twenty seven? Three times three times three. So it is three.

steps.title: Find the power of a fractional base
steps.narration: Now the hard one, log base one quarter of sixty four. What power of a quarter gives sixty four? A quarter makes things smaller, but sixty four is big. So the power must be negative. A negative power flips the quarter to four. Four cubed is sixty four. So the answer is minus three.

steps.title: Find the denominator
steps.narration: Now the bottom, log three of one over eighty one. Three to the four is eighty one. But we want one over eighty one, which is a flip. Flipping means a negative power. So the answer is minus four.

steps.title: Keep both negative signs
steps.narration: Now put it together, and watch the signs. On top, three minus minus three. Two minuses make a plus, so that is six. On the bottom, minus four. Six over minus four simplifies to minus three over two. Most wrong answers come from losing one of these minus signs.

steps.title: Halve the argument using division inside the log
steps.narration: Here is a trap. Log of five is not half of log of ten. Halving the number inside does not halve the log. Instead, think of five as ten divided by two. That gives log of ten minus log of two. Log base eight of two is one third, because the cube root of eight is two.

steps.title: Check the sign of a reciprocal power
steps.narration: Be careful with fractions inside a log. One over eighty one is smaller than one. To get a small number from three, you need a negative power. So log three of one over eighty one is minus four, not four. Ask yourself, is the answer bigger or smaller than one? That tells you the sign.

steps.title: Remember this
steps.narration: So remember the main idea. A log gives you a power. Whenever a log feels hard, ask what power of the base gives this number. Use the rules to combine logs, check the allowed values, and watch your signs. Logs then become simple power questions.

options.why: The three powers are 3, 4 and 2 exactly. Their signed sum is 5, so there is no rounding to 6.
The two positive terms add to 7. Subtracting 2 gives 5.
Four is the middle logarithm alone. The other terms contribute 3 − 2 = 1.

steps.title: Picture it
steps.narration: Imagine bundles of sticks tied in pairs. Pull out the complete pairs first, then see which loose bundles have the same label and can go together.

steps.title: Take perfect squares out of roots
steps.narration: A surd is a root that won't come out as a whole number, like root two. To simplify one, look for a perfect square hiding inside. Seventy two is thirty six times two. Thirty six is a perfect square, and its root is six. So root seventy two becomes six root two. The six comes out, and the two stays inside.

steps.title: Add and subtract like surds
steps.narration: You can only add surds that are the same kind. Think of them like oranges. Three oranges plus two oranges is five oranges. So three root two plus two root two is five root two. But root two and root three are different fruits. Sometimes they only look different, so simplify first. Root eighteen and root eight are both secretly root two.

steps.title: Multiply and divide under the root
steps.narration: For multiplying, roots can join under one roof. Root two times root three is root six. Multiply the outside numbers together, and the inside numbers together. Two root three times three root six gives six root eighteen. Then simplify. Root eighteen is three root two, so the answer is eighteen root two.

steps.title: Clear a single root from the denominator
steps.narration: JAMB likes answers without a root on the bottom. How do we remove it? Multiply the top and the bottom by the same root. Root two times root two is just two. So three over root two becomes three root two over two. The value hasn't changed, because we multiplied by one in disguise.

steps.title: Clear a two-term denominator with its conjugate
steps.narration: When the bottom has two terms, like three plus root two, one root won't fix it. Use the conjugate. Just flip the sign in the middle. Three plus root two becomes three minus root two. Multiply them, and the roots cancel out. You get nine minus two, which is seven. No root left on the bottom.

steps.title: Look for square factors
steps.narration: Let's try one. Before doing anything, look for perfect squares inside each root. Forty five is nine times five, so root forty five is three root five. Twenty is four times five, so root twenty is two root five. Now they are both root fives. Same fruit.

steps.title: Subtract the coefficients
steps.narration: Now the top is easy. Three root five minus two root five is just one root five. Like three oranges minus two oranges leaves one orange. So the whole top becomes root five.

steps.title: Cancel the remaining root
steps.narration: Root five over root five. Anything divided by itself is one. So the answer is simply one. See how simplifying first made this easy? Without it, you would be stuck with three different roots.

steps.title: Choose a conjugate
steps.narration: Now a real JAMB question. The bottom has two terms, root two plus root three. So we need a conjugate. Flip the middle sign. Here is a nice choice. Use root three minus root two. Multiplying gives three minus two, which is just one. A bottom of one is the best we can get.

steps.title: Multiply both parts of the fraction
steps.narration: Multiply both the top and the bottom by root three minus root two. The bottom becomes one, so the fraction disappears. Now we only need to expand the top. Take it slowly. Each term in the first bracket multiplies each term in the second.

steps.title: Collect the like terms
steps.narration: Expand carefully. Two root two times root three is two root six. Two root two times minus root two is minus four. Minus root three times root three is minus three. Minus root three times minus root two is plus root six. Now collect. Two root six plus root six is three root six. Minus four minus three is minus seven.

steps.title: Simplify before subtracting
steps.narration: Never subtract the numbers inside roots directly. Root one hundred and forty seven minus root twelve is not root one hundred and thirty five. Simplify each one first. One hundred and forty seven is forty nine times three, giving seven root three. Twelve gives two root three. Now subtract. Five root three.

steps.title: Keep the signs when expanding
steps.narration: When expanding brackets, the signs are where marks are lost. Minus root three times root three is minus three, not plus three. Minus times plus is minus. Say each sign out loud as you go. So it is minus four minus three, which is minus seven, not minus one.

steps.title: Remember this
steps.narration: So here is the surd habit. Simplify every root first by pulling out perfect squares. Then you can see which ones are the same kind. Add or take away only matching roots. And use the conjugate to clear a two term bottom. Simplify first, and surds behave.

options.why: The conjugate gives 3^{2} − 5 = 4 in the denominator, so 2 is too small.
Multiplying by 3 + \sqrt{5} above and below gives (1 − \sqrt{5}) divided by 4.
The original numerator is negative and its denominator is positive, so a positive result cannot match.
The root terms in the numerator are 2\sqrt{5} − 3\sqrt{5}, giving −\sqrt{5}.

steps.title: Picture it
steps.narration: You have six oranges and nine mangoes. Make three identical bags with two oranges and three mangoes each. Factoring spots what every bag has in common.

steps.title: Take out a common factor by grouping
steps.narration: Factorising is multiplying backwards. Look for something every term shares, and take it out front. Six x squared plus nine x both share three x. Take it out, and three x times two x plus three is left. With four terms, group them in pairs. Each pair gives the same bracket, and that bracket comes out too.

steps.title: Recognise special factors
steps.narration: Some shapes are worth memorising, because JAMB loves them. Anything squared minus anything squared splits into a minus bracket and a plus bracket. Nine x squared minus twenty five is three x squared minus five squared. So it becomes three x minus five, times three x plus five. Spot the squares, and the answer writes itself.

steps.title: Split the middle term and solve
steps.display: ax^{2} + bx + c = ax^{2} + mx + nx + c
steps.narration: For a quadratic, split the middle term into two pieces. Multiply the first and last numbers. For two x squared plus seven x plus three, that is six. Now find two numbers that multiply to six and add to seven. Six and one. Split the seven x into six x and x, then group in pairs.

steps.title: Use the quadratic formula and discriminant
steps.narration: When the numbers won't split nicely, use the formula. It always works. The part under the root is called the discriminant, and it tells you a lot. If it is positive, there are two roots. If it is zero, there is just one. If it is negative, there are no real roots at all.

sources.where: The quadratic formula and the discriminant

steps.title: Link the roots to the coefficients
working: ax^{2} + bx + c = a(x − α)(x − β)
steps.narration: The roots hide inside the numbers of the quadratic. Add the two roots, and you get minus b over a. Multiply them, and you get c over a. Take x squared minus five x plus six. Its roots are two and three. Two plus three is five, and two times three is six. You can check roots in seconds this way.

steps.title: Get the remainder by substitution
working: x + 1 is a factor of P(x)
steps.narration: Want the remainder without long division? Just substitute. To divide by x plus one, put x equals minus one into the expression. Whatever comes out is the remainder. If you get zero, there is no remainder, so x plus one is a factor. This is the remainder theorem, and it saves a lot of time.

steps.title: Put zero on one side
steps.narration: Let's try one. To solve a quadratic, everything must be on one side, with zero on the other. Why? Because if two things multiply to zero, one of them must be zero. So move the x and the six across. We get two x squared minus x minus six equals zero.

steps.title: Find two numbers to split the middle
steps.narration: Multiply the first and last numbers. Two times minus six is minus twelve. Now find two numbers that multiply to minus twelve and add to minus one. Try three and minus four. Three times minus four is minus twelve, and they add to minus one. So split the middle into three x and minus four x.

steps.title: Group and read off the roots
steps.narration: Group in pairs. The first pair gives x times two x plus three. The second pair gives minus two times two x plus three. Both have the same bracket, so take it out. Now one of the brackets must be zero. So x is two, or x is minus three over two.

steps.title: Turn the known root into a factor
steps.display: One root of x^{3} − 2x^{2} − 5x + 6 = 0 is 1. Find the other roots.
steps.narration: Now a JAMB question with a cubic. We are told one root is one. Check it. One minus two minus five plus six is zero. It works. And if one is a root, then x minus one must be a factor. That is the key that unlocks the rest.

steps.title: Remove the known factor by grouping
steps.narration: Now pull x minus one out of the cubic. Split each term so x minus one appears every time. Group the terms, and x minus one comes out of each group. What is left is a simple quadratic, x squared minus x minus six. The hard cubic has become an easy quadratic.

steps.title: Factor the remaining quadratic
steps.narration: Now factorise x squared minus x minus six. We need two numbers that multiply to minus six and add to minus one. Minus three and two. So it becomes x minus three, times x plus two.

steps.title: Set the remaining factors to zero
steps.narration: Each bracket can be zero. So x is three, or x is minus two. With the root we were given, the three roots are one, three and minus two. Always check one of them in the original. Put in three, and twenty seven minus eighteen minus fifteen plus six gives zero.

steps.title: Keep the entire second square in brackets
steps.narration: This trap is about brackets. One minus a minus b, all squared, is a difference of two squares. But the second square is the whole of a minus b. Keep it in a bracket. When you open it, the minus sign changes every sign inside. Students who drop the bracket get the signs wrong.

steps.title: Substitute the root, with its correct sign
steps.narration: If x minus four is a factor, which number do you put in? Four, not minus four. Set the bracket to zero. X minus four equals zero gives x equals four. Many students put in minus four and get the wrong value of k. Always solve the bracket first, then substitute.

steps.title: Remember this
steps.display: Use the product to find the roots
steps.narration: So here is the factorising habit. Get zero on one side first. Then break the expression into brackets that multiply together. If the product is zero, one bracket must be zero. Each bracket gives you a root. Check one root in the original, and you are done.

quickCheck.stem: For which p does x^{2} − (p−2)x + 2p + 1 = 0 have equal roots?

options.why: The discriminant is (p − 2)^{2} − 4(2p + 1) = p(p − 12), so it vanishes at 0 and 12.
Neither 1 nor 2 makes p(p − 12) equal to zero.
Zero works, but 21 leaves a nonzero discriminant and gives two distinct roots.
Both 4 and 5 make p(p − 12) negative, so neither gives equal real roots.

steps.title: Picture it
steps.narration: Two bags each hold an orange and a mango. Open both bags and put oranges with oranges and mangoes with mangoes. Algebra sorts terms that way too.

steps.title: Expand, then collect matching terms
steps.narration: Expanding means every term in the first bracket meets every term in the second. Nobody gets left out. For x plus two, times x minus three, x meets x and minus three. Then two meets x and minus three. Now collect the like terms. Minus three x plus two x leaves minus x.

steps.title: Cancel common factors and keep restrictions
steps.narration: You can only cancel things that multiply the whole top and the whole bottom. So factorise first. X squared minus four becomes x minus two, times x plus two. Now x minus two is on top and bottom, so it cancels. But remember, x can never be two, because the bottom would be zero.

steps.title: Use the appropriate fraction operation
working: Original denominators and any divisor must be nonzero.
steps.narration: Fractions in algebra follow the same rules as fractions with numbers. To add or take away, make the bottoms the same first. To multiply, go straight across, top times top and bottom times bottom. To divide, flip the second fraction and multiply. And the bottom is never allowed to be zero.

steps.title: Undo operations to change the subject
working: y = ax + bx + c ⇒ x = \frac{y − c}{a + b} (a + b ≠ 0)
steps.narration: Changing the subject is like unwrapping a parcel. Undo the last thing that was done first. If y equals a x plus b, the b was added last. So take away b first. Then x was multiplied by a, so divide by a. If x appears twice, gather the x terms together and factor x out.

steps.title: Solve two equations together
steps.narration: Two equations, two unknowns. The trick is to get rid of one unknown. Look at x plus y and x minus y. If you add them, the y's cancel out. Two x equals eight, so x is four. Then put four back in to find y, which is three. Always check both equations at the end.

steps.title: Substitute in a linear and quadratic system
steps.narration: When one equation is a quadratic, substitute. The first equation tells us y is two x. So replace y in the second equation with two x. Now there is only x, and it is a quadratic. Solve it to get two values of x. Then find y for each one. Each x gives its own y.

steps.title: Look for a variable to eliminate
steps.narration: Let's try one. Before working, look for an easy way to remove one unknown. In the first equation, y has a plus. In the second, y has a minus. So adding the two equations will cancel y completely.

steps.title: Find the first unknown
steps.narration: Add them. Two x plus x is three x. Plus y minus y is nothing. And eight plus one is nine. So three x equals nine, and x is three. One unknown found.

steps.title: Substitute and check the pair
steps.narration: Now put three into the easier equation. Three minus y equals one, so y is two. Check both. Two times three plus two gives eight. Three minus two gives one. Both work, so the pair is right.

steps.title: Keep the original restrictions
steps.narration: Now a JAMB question. It looks like a mess of x squareds. But the plan is simple. Factorise everything, then cancel matching brackets. And notice the question gives the values x can't be. Those values make a bottom zero.

steps.title: Factor each expression
steps.narration: Factorise each part. X squared minus nine is a difference of squares. That gives x minus three, times x plus three. X squared minus three x has x in common, so it is x times x minus three. X squared minus forty nine gives x minus seven, times x plus seven.

steps.title: Cancel matching factors
steps.narration: Now cancel brackets that appear on top and bottom. X minus seven is on top in the first fraction and on the bottom in the second. Cancel it. X minus three appears on top and bottom too. Cancel it. What is left is x, over x plus three, times x plus seven.

steps.title: Cancel the same bracket
steps.narration: Be careful which bracket you cancel. X minus three and x plus three look alike, but they are not the same. You can only cancel a bracket against an identical one. So the x plus three stays on the bottom. Check each cancel with your finger.

steps.title: Collect terms with their signs
steps.narration: When you move terms across, each one carries its sign with it. Moving minus w c n to the other side makes it plus. Moving v c n across makes it minus. Then factor out c n. Getting one sign wrong flips the whole answer.

steps.title: Answer what the question asks for
steps.narration: Read the question again before you choose. Sometimes it does not want x or y. It wants something made from them, like x plus y. If x is five and y is minus three, then x plus y is two. JAMB often puts five in the options to catch you.

steps.title: Remember this
steps.narration: So remember the golden rule of algebra. An equation is a balance. Whatever you do to one side, do to the other. Keep the signs with their terms. Factorise before you cancel. And always check your answer in the original equation.

quickCheck.stem: Make g the subject of gt^{2} − k − w = 0, with t ≠ 0.

options.why: Both k and w are added to the other side, and the coefficient of g is t^{2}.
Adding k and w and dividing by the nonzero coefficient t^{2} isolates g.
The denominator is right, but moving −w requires adding w to both sides.
The coefficient multiplying g is t^{2}, so dividing by t alone leaves another factor of t.

steps.title: Picture it
steps.display: How steep is the hill here?
steps.narration: Imagine cycling up a hill that gets steeper and then flattens out. Differentiation tells you how steep the road is just where your front wheel sits.

steps.title: Find the slope from first principles
steps.narration: Differentiation measures steepness at a single point. But one point alone can't give a slope. So take two points very close together and find the slope between them. Then let the gap shrink to zero. For x squared, the slope between the points is two x plus h. As h shrinks away, it becomes two x.

steps.title: Differentiate powers term by term
working: y′(x_{0}) is the tangent gradient at x_{0}
steps.narration: There is a quick rule for powers. Bring the power down to the front, then reduce the power by one. X cubed becomes three x squared. Do this to each term separately. A number on its own, like five, has no slope, so it disappears. The result tells you the steepness anywhere on the curve.

steps.title: Use the product rule
steps.narration: When two expressions multiply, use the product rule. Differentiate the first and keep the second. Then keep the first and differentiate the second. Add the two. For x times x squared plus one, that gives one times x squared plus one, plus x times two x. Altogether, three x squared plus one.

steps.title: Use the quotient rule
steps.narration: For one expression divided by another, use the quotient rule. Bottom times the top's slope, minus top times the bottom's slope, all over the bottom squared. Many students say low d high minus high d low, over low squared. The minus sign makes the order important.

steps.title: Use the chain rule for a function inside a function
working: (sin x)′ = cos x; (cos x)′ = −sin x; (tan x)′ = sec^{2} x
steps.narration: When something is inside a bracket, use the chain rule. Differentiate the outside first, leaving the inside alone. Then multiply by the slope of the inside. For two x plus one, cubed, the outside gives three times the bracket squared. The inside, two x plus one, has slope two. Multiply them together.

steps.title: Find and classify stationary points
steps.display: f′(c) = 0; f′′(c) < 0 gives a local maximum
working: f′ changes from + to − for a maximum, and from − to + for a minimum
Interior critical points have a zero or undefined derivative
steps.narration: At the top of a hill or the bottom of a valley, the ground is flat for a moment. So the slope is zero there. To find these points, set the derivative to zero and solve. Then check which one it is. Differentiate again. If the answer is negative, it is a top. If it is positive, it is a bottom.

steps.title: Find the gradient function
steps.display: Find the gradient of y = 2x^{3} − 5x + 1 at x = 2.
steps.narration: Let's try one. We want the steepness at x equals two. First, find the steepness everywhere. Two x cubed becomes six x squared. Minus five x becomes minus five. The plus one disappears. So the slope is six x squared minus five.

steps.title: Use the specified point
steps.narration: Now put in x equals two. Be careful with the order here. Square the two first, then multiply by six. Two squared is four, so we need six times four, minus five. Doing the multiplying first avoids a common slip.

steps.title: Read the slope
steps.narration: Six times four is twenty four. Take away five, and we get nineteen. So at x equals two, the curve rises nineteen units for every one unit across. That is a very steep part of the curve, and nineteen is our answer.

steps.title: Expand the quadratic
steps.display: At what x does f(x) = x(4 − x) reach its maximum?
steps.narration: Now a JAMB question. We want the highest point of x times four minus x. A bracket like this is hard to differentiate. So expand it first. X times four is four x. X times minus x is minus x squared.

steps.title: Find the horizontal tangent
steps.narration: At the highest point, the curve is flat, so the slope is zero. Differentiate four x minus x squared. You get four minus two x. Set it to zero. Four minus two x equals zero, so x is two.

steps.title: Check that it is the maximum
steps.narration: Is it really the highest point, or the lowest? Differentiate again. Four minus two x becomes minus two. Negative means the curve bends downwards, like a hill. So x equals two gives the maximum.

steps.title: Keep the inner derivative
steps.narration: The chain rule trap. Students differentiate the outside and forget the inside. For two x plus one, cubed, three times the bracket squared is only half the job. You must multiply by the slope of the inside, which is two. So the answer is six times the bracket squared.

steps.title: Track both minus signs
steps.narration: Negative powers have two minus signs to watch. X to the minus one becomes minus one times x to the minus two. But there was already a minus in front of it. Minus times minus is plus. So the term becomes plus one over x squared. Say each sign as you write it.

steps.title: Remember this
steps.narration: Remember the big idea. The derivative is the slope. It tells you how steep the curve is at any point. Where it is zero, the curve is flat, and that is a maximum or minimum. Learn the power rule well, and most of differentiation follows.

options.why: Multiplying by the old powers gives 12x^{2} and −4x, and differentiating x gives 1.
The cubic needs a multiplier of 3, and the quadratic needs a multiplier of 2.
The cubic contributes 4 × 3, so the first coefficient is 12.
The term −2x^{2} contributes −2 × 2 × x, so its derivative is −4x.

steps.title: Picture it
steps.display: Build the whole from thin strips
steps.narration: Imagine covering a curved patch of ground with strips of paper. Thinner strips fit the edge better. An integral gives the exact total as the strips get thinner.

steps.title: Reverse differentiation
steps.display: F′(x) = f(x) ⇒ ∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + C on an interval
steps.narration: Integration is differentiation backwards. Differentiation takes a curve and gives its slope. Integration takes the slope and finds the curve. But there is a catch. Constants disappear when you differentiate, so we don't know what was there. That is why we always add plus C. If the question gives a point, use it to find C.

steps.title: Add one to the power, then divide
steps.narration: Here is the reverse of the power rule. Make the power one bigger, then divide by that new power. X squared becomes x cubed over three. So six x squared becomes two x cubed. A plain number like four becomes four x. One power breaks this rule. One over x integrates to the natural log of x.

steps.title: Check simple substitutions by differentiating
working: ∫ sin x dx = −cos x + C; ∫ cos x dx = sin x + C; ∫ sec^{2} x dx = tan x + C
steps.narration: When there is a bracket like two x inside, integrate as normal. Then divide by the number in front of x. Why divide? Because differentiating would multiply by it, so integrating must undo that. Cos of two x becomes half sin of two x. You can always check by differentiating your answer.

steps.title: Use upper value minus lower value
steps.narration: A definite integral has numbers at the top and bottom. Integrate first, then put in the top number, then the bottom number. Always top minus bottom. For two x from one to three, the integral is x squared. Three squared is nine, one squared is one. Nine minus one gives eight.

steps.title: Use nonnegative heights for area
working: A = ∫_{a}^{b} (upper − lower) dx when their order stays fixed
A between y = x and the axis on [−1, 1] is \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} = 1
steps.narration: Area is always positive, but an integral can be negative. Below the x axis, the integral comes out negative. So split the region where the curve crosses the axis, and count each part as positive. Between two curves, take the upper curve minus the lower curve, then integrate that height.

steps.title: Find an antiderivative
steps.display: A curve has gradient 4x − 3 and passes through (1, 2). Find its equation.
steps.narration: Let's try one. We are given the gradient, and we want the curve. That is integration. Integrate each term. Four x becomes two x squared. Minus three becomes minus three x. And never forget plus C, because we don't know the constant yet.

steps.title: Use the point to find the constant
steps.narration: Now use the point. The curve passes through one, two. So when x is one, y is two. Put those in. Two times one, minus three, plus C, equals two. That is minus one plus C equals two. So C is three.

steps.title: Write and check the curve
steps.narration: So the curve is y equals two x squared minus three x plus three. Let's check both facts. Differentiate it, and you get four x minus three. That matches the gradient. Put in x equals one, and you get two. That matches the point. Both checks pass.

steps.title: Find where the curves meet
steps.display: Find the area bounded by y = 4 − x^{2} and y = 2x + 1.
steps.narration: Now a JAMB question about area between two curves. First, where do the curves meet? Set them equal. Four minus x squared equals two x plus one. Move everything to one side and factorise. They meet at x equals minus three and x equals one. Those are our limits.

steps.title: Find the upper curve
steps.narration: Which curve is on top? Test a number between the limits. Zero is easy. The first curve gives four, and the line gives one. So the curve is on top. The height of the region is the curve minus the line. That simplifies to three minus two x minus x squared.

steps.title: Integrate the height
steps.narration: Now integrate the height. Three becomes three x. Minus two x becomes minus x squared. Minus x squared becomes minus x cubed over three. We will put in the limits next, top first.

steps.title: Subtract the lower value
steps.narration: Put in the top limit, one. Three minus one minus a third gives five thirds. Put in the bottom limit, minus three. That gives minus nine. Now top minus bottom. Five thirds minus minus nine. Two minuses make a plus, so the area is thirty two over three.

steps.title: Keep the sign of a definite integral
steps.narration: Always put the top number in first. Top minus bottom, never bottom minus top. If you swap them, the sign flips, and JAMB will have that wrong answer waiting. For this one, the correct value is minus eleven thirds. The minus sign is part of the answer.

steps.title: Divide by the inner slope
steps.narration: With a bracket like two x plus three, integrate as normal, then divide by two. Students often forget this last step. The power goes up to three over two, and you divide by three over two. Then divide by two again for the inside. That gives one third, not two thirds.

steps.title: Remember this
steps.display: Reverse the derivative and use the given information
steps.narration: So remember this. Integration reverses differentiation. Add one to the power and divide by it. Always add plus C, and use any given point to find it. For areas, use top minus bottom, and the upper curve minus the lower one. Check by differentiating whenever you can.

quickCheck.stem: A curve has gradient 6x − 5 at every point and passes through (2, 5). Find its equation.

options.why: Its derivative is 12x − 5, so the coefficient of x squared is too large.
Its derivative is 12x + 5, so both derivative terms differ from the given gradient.
The derivative is right, but substituting x = 2 gives −3 instead of 5.
Its derivative is 6x − 5 and substituting x = 2 gives 12 − 10 + 3 = 5.

steps.title: Picture it
steps.display: Walk it, cover it, fill it
steps.narration: Walk round a garden to measure its edge, lay mats to cover the ground, or fill a bucket with water. Each job measures something different.

steps.title: Add lengths for the distance round
steps.narration: Perimeter is the distance around the edge, like walking round a field. Just add up every side. A rectangle has two lengths and two widths. So a five by three rectangle has perimeter sixteen. For a circle, the distance round is called the circumference. It is two pi times the radius.

steps.title: Measure flat area with the correct height
steps.narration: Area is how much flat space a shape covers, like tiles on a floor. The key is using the right height. The height must stand straight up from the base, at a right angle. A slanted side is not the height. A triangle is half of a rectangle. So with base eight and height three, the area is twelve.

steps.title: Take the right fraction of a circle
steps.narration: A sector is a slice of a circle, like a slice of pizza. What fraction of the whole circle is it? Divide its angle by three hundred and sixty. Then take that fraction of the full circumference for the curved edge. Take that fraction of the full area for the area. A ninety degree slice is one quarter.

sources.where: Calculation Notes, Sectors and Areas of segments

steps.title: Find the area and boundary of a segment
steps.narration: A segment is the part between a chord and the curved edge. Think of it as the slice with the triangle cut away. So find the sector area, then take away the triangle. The triangle's area is half r squared times sine of the angle. For the perimeter, add the curved edge and the straight chord.
working: L_{chord} = 2r sin(\frac{θ}{2}); P_{minor segment} = L_{arc} + L_{chord}

sources.where: Calculation Notes, Sectors and Areas of segments

steps.title: Use the base area for volume
working: B = 6 cm^{2}, h = 8 cm ⇒ V_{prism} = 48 cm^{3}
steps.narration: Volume is how much a solid can hold. For any prism or cylinder, find the area of the end. Then multiply by the length. It is like stacking many thin slices. A pointed solid, like a cone or pyramid, holds exactly one third of that. So remember to divide by three for pointed shapes.

sources.where: Surface area of a right pyramid, Surface area of a cone, and The sphere

steps.title: Add the exposed surfaces
working: S_{cuboid} = 2(lw + lh + wh); S_{prism} = 2B + P_{base}h for a right prism
ℓ = \sqrt{r^{2} + h^{2}} for a right cone
steps.narration: Surface area is the total area of every face you could paint. Add up all the outside surfaces. A closed cylinder has a curved side plus two circles. A cone has a curved side plus one circle at the bottom. Read the question carefully. An open container has no top, so leave that face out.

sources.where: Surface area of a right pyramid, Surface area of a cone, and The sphere

steps.title: Use the triangle at the end
steps.display: A right triangular prism is 5 cm long. Its right-angled end has perpendicular sides 3 cm and 4 cm. Find its volume.
steps.narration: Let's try one. A prism is the same shape all the way through. So first find the area of its end. Here the end is a right angled triangle. The two short sides are three and four, and they meet at a right angle. So they act as base and height. Half of three times four gives six.

steps.title: Extend that area through the prism
steps.narration: Now stretch that end through the whole length of the prism. Every slice has an area of six. The prism is five long. So the volume is six times five.

steps.title: Give the volume in cubic units
steps.narration: Six times five is thirty. Since we multiplied an area by a length, the unit is cubic centimetres. So the volume is thirty cubic centimetres. Check the unit in the options, because JAMB sometimes swaps square and cubic units.

steps.title: Find the fraction of a full turn
steps.display: A 45° sector of a circle has radius 8 cm. What is its perimeter?
steps.narration: Now a JAMB question about a sector. Its angle is forty five degrees. What fraction of a full turn is that? Forty five out of three hundred and sixty. Simplify, and it is one eighth. So this slice is one eighth of the circle.

steps.title: Find the curved edge
steps.narration: The curved edge is one eighth of the full distance round. The full circumference is two pi times eight, which is sixteen pi. One eighth of sixteen pi is two pi. So the curved edge is two pi centimetres.

steps.title: Include the straight edges
steps.narration: But a slice of pizza has more than a curved edge. It also has two straight edges, going to the centre. Each straight edge is the radius, eight. So the perimeter is two pi plus eight plus eight. That makes sixteen plus two pi centimetres.

steps.title: Count the whole sector boundary
steps.display: Wrong  P = 2π cm     |     Right  P = (16 + 2π) cm
steps.narration: This is the most common sector mistake. Students find the curved edge and stop. But the perimeter goes all the way round the slice. That includes the two straight radii. Imagine walking round the edge of the pizza slice. You walk the curve, then both straight sides.

steps.title: Use the area of the actual prism end
steps.display: Right triangular end with perpendicular sides 3 cm and 4 cm
steps.narration: If the end of a prism is a triangle, use the triangle's area. Do not multiply all three lengths as if it were a box. A right triangle with sides three and four has area six, not twelve. Then times eight gives forty eight. A box formula would give ninety six, which is double.

steps.title: Remember this
steps.display: Match the formula to what is measured
steps.narration: So here is the main idea. First ask what is being measured. Distance round is perimeter, in plain units. Flat space is area, in square units. Space inside is volume, in cubic units. Choose the formula that matches, and check the unit in your answer.

quickCheck.stem: Find the area of a sector with centre angle 70° and radius 6 cm. Use π ≈ \frac{22}{7}.

options.why: The specified fraction of the circle area is (70 ÷ 360) × (22 ÷ 7) × 36, which is 22 cm^{2}.
This is twice the sector area. The sector takes only 70 out of the full 360 degrees.
This is three times the sector area. The angle fraction must be 70 divided by 360.
This is four times the sector area. Multiplying the circle area by 70 divided by 360 gives 22.

steps.title: Picture it
steps.display: Two ways to grow a pile
steps.narration: Start with a pile of sweets. In one game you add two each round. In another you double the pile. Both patterns are predictable.

steps.title: Recognise an arithmetic progression by its difference
steps.narration: In an arithmetic progression, you add the same number each time. That number is the common difference. Three, seven, eleven goes up by four each time. To get the fifth term, start at three and add four, four times. That gives nineteen. Why four times and not five? The first term already counts as one.

steps.title: Sum an arithmetic progression by pairing ends
steps.narration: Here is a lovely trick for adding an arithmetic progression. Pair the first term with the last. Then pair the second with the second last. Every pair adds to the same total. So count the pairs, and multiply. For three, seven, eleven, fifteen, each pair makes eighteen. Two pairs make thirty six.

steps.title: Recognise a geometric progression by its ratio
steps.narration: In a geometric progression, you multiply by the same number each time. That number is the common ratio. Four, twelve, thirty six multiplies by three each time. To get the fourth term, start at four and multiply by three, three times. That gives one hundred and eight. Again, one fewer than the term number.

steps.title: Sum a finite geometric progression
steps.narration: To add a geometric progression, use the sum formula. It comes from a neat trick of multiplying the whole sum by r and subtracting. For two, six, eighteen, the ratio is three. Three cubed is twenty seven. So the sum is two times one minus twenty seven, over one minus three. That gives twenty six.

steps.title: Sum an infinite geometric progression when it converges
steps.narration: Some progressions go on forever but still have a total. This only happens when each term gets smaller, so the ratio is between minus one and one. Six, three, one and a half keeps halving. The terms get tiny, and the total settles at twelve. The formula is the first term over one minus the ratio.

steps.title: Check how the terms change
steps.display: Find the sum of the first four terms of 3, 6, 12, … .
steps.narration: Let's try one. Before choosing a formula, find out what kind of progression it is. Is it adding or multiplying? Six divided by three is two. Twelve divided by six is two. The same ratio each time, so it is geometric, with ratio two.

steps.title: Use the finite sum rule
steps.narration: Now use the geometric sum formula. The first term is three, the ratio is two, and we want four terms. So it is three times one minus two to the four, over one minus two. Keep the brackets so the signs stay safe.

steps.title: Simplify and check by listing
steps.narration: Two to the four is sixteen, and one minus sixteen is minus fifteen. On the bottom, one minus two is minus one. Three times minus fifteen over minus one gives forty five. Check by listing the terms. Three, six, twelve, twenty four. They add to forty five.

steps.title: Count the jumps between the terms
steps.display: The fourth term of an arithmetic progression is 13 and the tenth is 31. Find the twenty-fourth term.
steps.narration: Now a JAMB question. We know the fourth term and the tenth term. How many jumps are between them? Ten minus four gives six jumps. And the value grew from thirteen to thirty one. That is eighteen. So six jumps added eighteen.

steps.title: Work out the common difference
steps.narration: If six jumps added eighteen, then each jump adds eighteen divided by six. That is three. So the common difference is three. We found it without needing the first term at all.

steps.title: Jump from the known fourth term
steps.narration: Now jump from the fourth term to the twenty fourth. That is twenty jumps. Each jump adds three, so twenty jumps add sixty. Thirteen plus sixty gives seventy three. That is the twenty fourth term.

steps.title: Count multiplications from the first term
steps.narration: Count the multiplications carefully. To reach the eleventh term, you start at the first and multiply ten times, not eleven. The first term needs no multiplying at all. So it is four times two to the ten. Using two to the eleven gives an answer twice too big.

steps.title: Divide by one minus the ratio
steps.narration: For an infinite sum, you divide. You don't take away. One plus nine tenths plus more terms, forever. First work out one minus nine tenths, which is one tenth. Then divide the first term by it. One divided by one tenth is ten. So the sum is ten, not one tenth.

steps.title: Remember this
steps.display: Check the change from term to term
steps.narration: So for every progression question, start with one check. Look at how each term changes into the next. If you add the same amount, it is arithmetic. If you multiply by the same amount, it is geometric. Then choose the matching formula, and count the jumps carefully.

quickCheck.stem: Find the sum to infinity of 1 + \frac{9}{10} + (\frac{9}{10})^{2} + (\frac{9}{10})^{3} + … .

options.why: One tenth is the denominator in the sum formula, so the sum is 1 divided by one tenth.
Nine tenths is the common ratio. The sum already exceeds 1 after adding its first two terms.
This divides the first term by the ratio instead of by 1 minus the ratio.
The ratio is nine tenths, so the infinite sum is 1 ÷ (1 − 0.9) = 10.

steps.title: Picture it
steps.narration: A tray holds a hundred pieces of chin-chin. Take twenty five. That is twenty five percent. It is also a quarter, or zero point two five.

steps.title: Add or subtract equal-sized parts
steps.narration: You can only add fractions when the pieces are the same size. A half and a third are different sizes. So cut them into sixths. A half becomes three sixths, and a third becomes two sixths. Now add the pieces. Five sixths. With mixed numbers, turn them into top heavy fractions first.

steps.title: Multiply fractions and divide by the reciprocal
steps.narration: Multiplying fractions is the easy one. Top times top, bottom times bottom. Dividing has one extra step. Flip the second fraction, then multiply. Why flip? Dividing by a quarter means asking how many quarters fit, and that is the same as times four. So two thirds divided by four fifths is two thirds times five quarters.

steps.title: Use place value for decimals
steps.narration: Decimals are fractions with bottoms of ten, hundred or thousand. Zero point two five is twenty five hundredths, which is a quarter. When multiplying decimals, count the decimal places. Zero point three times zero point zero four has three decimal places, so zero point zero one two. When dividing, move both points until you divide by a whole number.

steps.title: Round at the requested place
steps.narration: Read the rounding instruction carefully. Significant figures start counting from the first digit that is not zero. Decimal places count from the decimal point. So the same number rounds differently. Zero point zero zero seven eight four six becomes zero point zero zero seven eight five to three significant figures. To three decimal places, it is zero point zero zero eight.

sources.book: Cambridge Excellence in Mathematics Senior Secondary 2 Student’s Book

steps.title: Use the original amount as the percent base
steps.narration: Percentage change always compares with the original amount, the starting value. Find the change, divide by the original, then times one hundred. For an increase of fifteen percent, multiply by one point one five. To go backwards and find the original, divide by one point one five instead. Never take fifteen percent off the new amount.

steps.title: Use the original principal for simple interest
steps.narration: Simple interest is paid only on the money you first put in. It does not grow on itself. Multiply the principal by the rate and the time. Two thousand naira at six percent for two years gives two hundred and forty naira. Add it to the principal for the total amount.

steps.title: Find the multiplier for an increase
steps.display: A bag costs ₦2,400 after a 20% increase. Find the original price.
steps.narration: Let's try one. The bag costs two thousand four hundred after a twenty percent rise. That price is not the original. It is the original times something. A twenty percent rise means the original times one point two.

steps.title: Undo the multiplication
steps.narration: So to go back to the original, undo the multiplication. Divide by one point two. Two thousand four hundred divided by one point two gives two thousand naira. That is the original price.

steps.title: Check using the original price
steps.narration: Let's check it. Twenty percent of two thousand is four hundred. Two thousand plus four hundred gives two thousand four hundred. That matches the new price, so our answer is right. Always check by going forwards again.

steps.title: Convert the mixed numbers
steps.narration: Now a JAMB question. There are three mixed numbers and three operations. Mixed numbers are hard to multiply. So change each one into a top heavy fraction first. Three and a third becomes ten thirds. One and a quarter becomes five quarters. One and two fifths becomes seven fifths.

steps.title: Do the multiplication first
steps.narration: Which operation comes first? Not left to right. Multiplication comes before adding and taking away. So do five quarters times two thirds first. That gives ten twelfths, which simplifies to five sixths.

steps.title: Use a common denominator
steps.narration: Now we have ten thirds, minus five sixths, plus seven fifths. Different bottoms, so find a common one. Thirty works for three, six and five. Ten thirds becomes one hundred thirtieths. Five sixths becomes twenty five thirtieths. Seven fifths becomes forty two thirtieths. That gives one hundred and seventeen thirtieths.

steps.title: Reduce the result
steps.narration: Now simplify. One hundred and seventeen and thirty both divide by three. That gives thirty nine tenths. As a mixed number, that is three and nine tenths. Check which form the options use before you choose.

steps.title: Multiply before subtracting
steps.narration: The big trap here is doing it left to right. If you take away first, you get the wrong answer. Multiplication must come before taking away. So work out five quarters times two thirds on its own first. Then do the rest. Put brackets round the multiplication if it helps you remember.

steps.title: Recover the original percentage base
steps.display: ₦345 is the salary after a 15% rise
steps.narration: Three hundred and forty five naira is the salary after a fifteen percent rise. To find the old salary, do not take fifteen percent off. That uses the wrong starting amount. Instead, divide by one point one five. That gives three hundred naira. Check it, and fifteen percent of three hundred is forty five.

steps.title: Remember this
steps.display: Track what counts as one whole
steps.narration: So for fractions and percentages, always ask one question. What counts as the whole? For fractions, make the pieces the same size before adding. For percentages, always measure from the original amount. Get the whole right, and the rest is simple arithmetic.

quickCheck.stem: Calculate the simple interest on ₦1,500 for 8 years at 5% per year.

options.why: ₦5,000 would exceed the original principal several times. The stated rate gives 0.05 × ₦1,500 = ₦75 a year, or ₦600 in eight years.
The annual interest is ₦75, so eight years gives 8 × ₦75 = ₦600.
₦500 falls short of the total because eight yearly payments of ₦75 add up to ₦600.
₦150 is only two years of interest at ₦75 per year.
